title: A psychoacoustical approach to resolving office noise distraction
research_question: To determine whether noise perception and distraction in the office are affected by psychological factors (personality type, perceived control, screening ability) and personal factors (age, primary workplace), rather than simply by physical metrics.

participants.description: Respondents from the UK (50.2%) and The Netherlands (18.6%), primarily from the construction industry (architects, designers, engineers, consultants/advisors). Primary workplaces included open-plan desks (53.9%), hot/flexi desks (17.3%), home (17.8%), private/shared offices (27%), and co-working spaces (1.3%).
participants.recruitment: Invited via email to potential conference delegates (Merlin Events and Marketing, Saint-Gobain Ecophon clients) and social media (LinkedIn groups, Twitter feeds).

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Respondents' self-reported primary workspace (e.g., open-plan desk, home office, private office) and their subjective experience of its noise levels and acoustic design.

mechanisms: Arousal theory (extroverts/introverts have different innate arousal levels affecting noise performance)
Cognitive resource depletion (neuroticism leads to reduced attentional resources due to internal worries)
Emotional response to unwanted sound (emotionally unstable individuals respond more negatively to noise, leading to stress)
Personality-based acceptance/desire for quiet (openness to new experiences may accept more noise, conscientious types desire fewer distractions)
Innate ability to 'screen' out noise (individual differences in coping with over-stimulation)
Perceived control over noise (higher control leads to less distraction and improved concentration)
Adaptation/coping strategies (people learn to cope with or adapt to noise levels, or work extra hours to compensate for lost productivity)
Allostatic load/stress (distractions causing inefficiencies lead to longer work hours, fatigue, stress, and absenteeism)
Cognitive load (unnecessary effort to deal with noise wastes physical and mental resources, affecting stress, well-being, and work efficiency)
moderators: Personality type (extroversion, neuroticism, conscientiousness, openness, agreeableness)
implementation_implications: Noise distraction solutions should be based on psychoacoustic, people-centred principles, not just physical metrics.
Acknowledge individual differences in noise perception; a single acoustic solution will not work for all.
Implement behavioural, educational, managerial, and organisational solutions in addition to physical ones.
Design office environments to provide a similar level of perceived control over noise as found in home settings.
Provide a range of work-settings to accommodate and separate noisy activities from quieter ones (Displace).
Minimize noise generation by design, e.g., avoid meeting tables near quiet workstations, locate noisy teams together (Avoid).
Limit noise distraction through good acoustic design (e.g., controlling desk size/density, reducing speech intelligibility) (Reduce).
Introduce office etiquette and reinforce expected behaviours in shared environments (Educate).

limitations: The size of effect for psychological and personal variables was smaller than anticipated, possibly due to the survey being conducted across a range of real-world workplaces with uncontrolled extraneous factors, rather than in a controlled laboratory setting.
In real-world settings, noise is one of many confounding factors, and motivational factors (e.g., reward, recognition) may have a larger impact on performance than physical environment factors.
The survey sample size, while sufficient for statistical analysis, was constraining for deeper investigation, and additional research is needed to further test the hypotheses.
The study was dependent on self-reported responses from a range of acoustic environments, without actual control over sound levels.

The finding that people still complete work despite distractions (maintaining perceived performance/productivity) might mask underlying inefficiencies, leading to longer work hours, fatigue, stress, and absenteeism.
